readings.title: Christmas Day: a carol, a peacock and Master Simon’s books
readings.challenge: Separate the narrator’s sincere admiration from his gentle mockery. Watch for the small comic details he lets fall in the middle of praise.
readings.focus: A morning of old customs, seen by a visitor who loves them and smiles at them at the same time.
readings.context: Old Christmas gathers five sketches from Washington Irving’s The Sketch Book (1819–20), in which an American traveller, Geoffrey Crayon, spends Christmas at Bracebridge Hall, the country house of an English squire who keeps up the customs of earlier centuries; this text follows an 1886 London edition. The household includes the Squire’s son Frank Bracebridge; Master Simon, a cheerful bachelor cousin who organises the festivities; a young Oxford student (“the Oxonian”); and the parson. Recap: in the earlier sketches the narrator met Frank Bracebridge, an old travelling companion, at a country inn, rode with him to the hall on Christmas Eve, and fell asleep to music after an evening of games and dancing. Herrick is Robert Herrick, a seventeenth-century poet of country festivals; Tusser, Fitzherbert and Markham wrote old books on farming, hunting and country life. A grandee is a Spanish nobleman of the highest rank; a hassock is a cushion for kneeling.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), “Christmas Day,” from the start through Frank Bracebridge’s description of the village choir; opens “When I awoke the next morning, it seemed as if all the events of the preceding evening…”; closes “…female singer being exceedingly wayward and capricious, and very liable to accident."”.

questions.prompt: The narrator sees a peacock strutting “with the pride and gravity of a Spanish grandee,” and later learns why the Squire keeps so many. What do the peacocks seem to stand for at Bracebridge Hall?
facilitatorNotes: They are birds of display that “belonged to chivalry” and suit “an old family mansion”: the Squire keeps them for the stateliness they lend his house. Master Simon’s old lore, that the peacock struts when praised and hides when his tail falls, makes the bird an emblem of pride.
Students may see a gentle joke at the hall’s love of show, or simply an affectionate picture of a house that values beauty and ceremony. Both readings use the same details.
evidence: strutting with the pride and gravity of a Spanish grandee
Nothing, he was accustomed to say, had an air of greater state and dignity than a peacock perched upon an antique stone balustrade.

questions.prompt: Master Simon corrects the narrator’s “flock” to “a muster of peacocks.” How does Irving mock Master Simon’s learning, and why is he still admired in the neighbourhood?
facilitatorNotes: His learning comes from “half-a-dozen old authors” that he reads “over and over” and quotes “with a kind of idolatry.” Among grooms and huntsmen, though, a man who can quote any book is “a prodigy of book-knowledge.”

The satire is affectionate: the narrator enjoys “the cheerful flow of animal spirits of the little man.” Readers may recognise the type, someone who knows a few sources very well and treats them as the last word.
evidence: with a slight air of pedantry
like all men who know but a few books, he looked up to them with a kind of idolatry, and quoted them on all occasions
a prodigy of book-knowledge by all the grooms, huntsmen, and small sportsmen of the neighbourhood

questions.prompt: Compare the narrator’s comments on the morning prayers with his report of the Squire’s views on breakfast. Where is he sincere, and where is he smiling?
facilitatorNotes: He states plainly that it is “much to be regretted” that morning household worship has declined, and he is moved by the Squire’s singing. But the claim that tea and toast cause “modern effeminacy and weak nerves” is reported with a straight face that invites laughter, and the Squire’s voice rambles “out of all the bounds of time and tune.”
Irving’s nostalgia and his comedy live side by side; students can mark which sentences belong to which. Some will hear irony even in the praise of worship.
evidence: it is much to be regretted that the custom is fallen into neglect
which he censured as among the causes of modern effeminacy and weak nerves
his voice rambling out of all the bounds of time and tune

readings.title: Christmas Day: the parson, the choir and a sermon against the Puritans
readings.challenge: Enjoy the comic portraits, then ask what each joke says about a person’s relation to the past.
readings.focus: A scholar who lives entirely in old books, and a church service that goes wrong and right at once.
readings.context: Recap: on Christmas morning the narrator heard children singing carols, joined family prayers, walked the grounds with Frank Bracebridge and Master Simon, and learned that Master Simon has trained a village choir. Black-letter is the heavy Gothic type of the first printed books, and Caxton and Wynkyn de Worde were among the first English printers. A “living” is a parson’s church post with its income; a sexton is a church caretaker. The Druids were priests of ancient Britain. In the 1640s and 1650s the Puritan-led Parliament banned the celebration of Christmas; it returned with King Charles II at the Restoration in 1660. William Prynne was a Puritan writer, and “Roundheads” were Parliament’s supporters.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), “Christmas Day,” from the walk to church through the greetings in the churchyard; opens “As the morning, though frosty, was remarkably fine and clear, the most of the family…”; closes “…the worthy old cavalier had not forgotten the true Christmas virtue of charity.”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator connect the parson’s appearance with his learning? Find the two comparisons that do the most work.
facilitatorNotes: His head shrinks inside his wig “like a dried filbert in its shell,” and his face looks like “a title-page of black-letter”: he has dried up among old books until he resembles one. He studies anything old “merely because it is denominated learning,” without asking whether it is wise or worthless.
The portrait is comic but not cruel. Students may notice that the narrator himself loves “odd and obsolete things,” so the joke is partly on a fellow antiquarian.
evidence: his head seemed to have shrunk away within it, like a dried filbert in its shell
if the face be an index of the mind, might be compared to a title-page of black-letter

questions.prompt: What makes the account of Master Simon’s anthem funny? Look at the comparisons the narrator borrows from hunting and battle.
facilitatorNotes: A fiddler races through bars “to be in at the death” like a fox-hunter; the chorus “Now let us sing with one accord” becomes “a signal for parting company”; and one old singer, lost in his own music, finishes alone with “a nasal solo.” The joke lies in the gap between the words being sung and the discord of the singing.
Readers might also notice how kindly the scene ends: the narrator never mocks the villagers’ effort, only the collapse of Master Simon’s great expectations.
evidence: which seemed to be a signal for parting company
winding all up by a nasal solo of at least three bars' duration

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator find the parson’s sermon unnecessary, and why does it work anyway?
facilitatorNotes: The parson argues, with a “mighty array” of Church Fathers, for keeping Christmas, a point nobody present disputes; he is still fighting the Puritans of two centuries before, because “the pages of old times were to him as the gazettes of the day.” Yet the congregation leaves “possessed with the gaiety of spirit” he urged.

The irony is double: an argument against imaginary opponents still produces a real effect. Students may also notice the narrator’s final observation, that the Squire has not forgotten “the true Christmas virtue of charity.”
evidence: I was a little at a loss to perceive the necessity of such a mighty array of forces to maintain a point which no one present seemed inclined to dispute
the pages of old times were to him as the gazettes of the day
I have seldom known a sermon attended apparently with more immediate effects

readings.title: Christmas Day: the Squire’s project and the sword-dance
readings.challenge: Read the Squire’s speech about the “peasantry” closely, then test it against the narrator’s small observations of real villagers.
readings.focus: Old customs as kindness, as nostalgia, and as a way of keeping the poor contented.
readings.context: Recap: after a learned sermon urging the congregation to keep Christmas merrily, the villagers greeted the Squire warmly and he invited them to the hall. The sketch was written in the hard years after the Napoleonic Wars, when English labourers suffered unemployment and high prices and many people were calling for “reform” of Parliament. Duke Humphry’s table meant going without dinner; “Squire Ketch” is the hangman. Brawn is pickled boar or pork; a Christmas-box collected gifts of money. The footnotes are Irving’s; the notes they mention are printed at the end of the book.
readings.contentNote: The Squire and the narrator speak of the rural poor with the condescension of their class and time.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), “Christmas Day,” from the walk home to the end of the sketch, with its footnotes; opens “On our way homeward his heart seemed overflowing with generous and happy feelings. As we…”; closes “[Footnote G: See Note D.]”.

questions.prompt: What does the Squire believe old games and customs did for England, and why does he want them back now?
facilitatorNotes: He says they made the peasant “fond of his home” and, when the gentry supported them, “fond of his lord.” Now the poor “begin to read newspapers” and “talk of reform,” and he hopes merry customs will keep them “in good humour in these hard times.” His nostalgia has a political purpose.

The narrator calls this “the good Squire’s project for mitigating public discontent,” a phrase that can be read as respectful or as quietly ironic. Students may judge the Squire generous, paternalistic, or both.
evidence: making the peasant fond of his home, and the promotion of them by the gentry made him fond of his lord
They have become too knowing, and begin to read newspapers, listen to alehouse politicians, and talk of reform.

questions.prompt: The Squire’s open house failed because the country people “did not understand how to play their parts.” What does that phrase suggest about his idea of hospitality?
facilitatorNotes: It treats the feast as a play in which the poor have assigned roles. Real vagrants and beggars did not follow the script, so now he invites only “the decent part” of the peasantry and sends food to the rest.
Some readers find the change sensible; others see that the revival of old hospitality works only when it is managed. The theatre image returns at the Christmas dinner and the masque.
evidence: did not understand how to play their parts in the scene of hospitality
inviting the decent part of the neighbouring peasantry

questions.prompt: After the dance, the narrator sees two or three young villagers wink at each other behind the Squire’s back. How does that detail sit beside his remark about the “gaiety of the lower orders”?
facilitatorNotes: He reports the grimace and their sudden “grave faces” when they catch his eye, and then generalises that the poor feel “genuine and affectionate” gratitude to their patrons. His own observation suggests some guests are humouring the Squire; they are “more at their ease” with Master Simon.
Students can decide whether the narrator notices the gap and lets it stand, or whether his generalisation simply overrides what he saw. Either way, the text gives evidence for a less rosy picture.
evidence: making something of a grimace, and giving each other the wink
There is something genuine and affectionate in the gaiety of the lower orders, when it is excited by the bounty and familiarity of those above them

readings.title: The Christmas Dinner: a boar’s head and the wassail bowl
readings.challenge: Notice every place where the old custom being revived turns out to be an imitation or a substitute, and how the household treats it.
readings.focus: An antique feast staged with real affection and a good deal of make-believe.
readings.context: Old Christmas gathers five sketches from Washington Irving’s The Sketch Book (1819–20), in which an American traveller, Geoffrey Crayon, spends Christmas at Bracebridge Hall, the country house of an English squire who keeps up the customs of earlier centuries; this text follows an 1886 London edition. The household includes the Squire’s son Frank Bracebridge; Master Simon, a cheerful bachelor cousin who organises the festivities; a young Oxford student (“the Oxonian”); and the parson. Recap: on Christmas Day the narrator went to church, heard the Squire praise old customs as a bond between rich and poor, and watched villagers perform a traditional sword-dance. This sketch follows the Christmas dinner itself. Belshazzar, in the Book of Daniel, held a feast with gold vessels taken from the Temple; Holbein and Dürer were Renaissance portrait artists. A train-band was a citizen militia. The Latin of the carol means “I bring the boar’s head, giving praise to the Lord … you who are at the feast.” Wassail is spiced ale or wine drunk in toasts; a toper is a heavy drinker. The bracketed letters mark Irving’s footnotes.
readings.contentNote: Drinking is part of the celebration.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), “The Christmas Dinner,” from the opening verses through Master Simon’s wassail song; opens “Lo, now is come the joyful'st feast! Let every man be jolly, Eache roome with yvie leaves…”; closes “…dost freely quaff-a, Sing, Fling, Be as merry as a king, And sound a lusty laugh-a.[M]”.

questions.prompt: The narrator has “strong doubts” that the painting and armour in the hall belonged to the crusader. How did they become accepted as his?
facilitatorNotes: The painting “had been so considered time out of mind,” and the Squire found the armour in a lumber room and “at once determined” it was the hero’s. Because he is “absolute authority” in his own house, his decision became accepted fact.
The detail shows that some of Bracebridge Hall’s antiquity is made, not inherited. Students might compare traditions they know that are younger than they look.
evidence: I had strong doubts about the authenticity of the painting and armour as having belonged to the crusader
as he was absolute authority on all such subjects in his own household, the matter had passed into current acceptation

questions.prompt: The “boar’s head” is a pig’s head and the peacock pie a pheasant pie. What do these substitutions show about the Squire’s revival of the past?
facilitatorNotes: The old feast can be imitated only “at humble distance”: the props stand in for the real thing, as the narrator says of the Squire’s other “makeshifts.” The pheasant pie also reveals kindness, since the Squire would not have a peacock killed after a bad season for them.
His family and servants play their parts as if after “many a rehearsal.” Readers may find the scene touching, comic, or both: a man reviving the past by staging it.
evidence: an enormous pig's head decorated with rosemary, with a lemon in its mouth
This the Squire confessed, with some little hesitation, was a pheasant-pie, though a peacock-pie was certainly the most authentical
the other makeshifts of this worthy old humorist

questions.prompt: The boar’s head carol makes the Squire remember Oxford and makes the parson correct the words. How do the two men respond differently to the same old song?
facilitatorNotes: For the Squire it calls up youth and friends, “many of whom, poor lads, are now in their graves”; for the parson, always “more taken up with the text than the sentiment,” it is a problem of the correct reading. His lecture shrinks to an “under voice” as his listeners drift away.
Ask which way of valuing the past the narrator seems to prefer. He gives the Squire feeling and the parson accuracy, and lets the parson’s audience vote with their attention.
evidence: many of whom, poor lads, are now in their graves!
who was always more taken up with the text than the sentiment
he lowered his tone as his number of auditors diminished

readings.title: The Christmas Dinner: college stories and blind-man’s buff
readings.challenge: Read the narrator’s theory of laughter, then watch how his own tone changes as the evening goes on.
readings.focus: Good humour, two old friends shaped by different lives, and a narrator whose amusement readers may not share.
readings.context: Recap: at the Christmas dinner a pig’s head was carried in as the medieval boar’s head, and the Squire’s wassail bowl went round the table while Master Simon sang. The Isis is the river at Oxford; a curricle is a light two-horse carriage. Joe Miller was the name on a famous old joke book. The Lord of Misrule presided over Christmas games in old great houses. In Shakespeare’s The Merry Wives of Windsor, children dressed as fairies pinch the fat knight Falstaff.
readings.contentNote: Heavy drinking. In a game of blind-man’s buff an elderly bachelor singles out a girl of thirteen, and the narrator presents it as amusing flirtation; readers today may find the scene uncomfortable.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), “The Christmas Dinner,” from the teasing of Master Simon through the game of blind-man’s buff; opens “Much of the conversation during dinner turned upon family topics, to which I was a…”; closes “…over chairs, I suspected the rogue of being not a whit more blinded than was convenient.”.

questions.prompt: “Wit, after all, is a mighty tart, pungent ingredient.” What does the narrator prefer to wit at a merry meeting, and why?
facilitatorNotes: He prefers “honest good humour,” where “the jokes are rather small, and the laughter abundant.” Wit can wound or exclude; good humour includes everyone, even the fat-headed old gentleman who forgets the ends of his stories.
Students may agree or argue that the evening sounds dull. The narrator admits he cannot “positively affirm that there was much wit uttered.”
evidence: Wit, after all, is a mighty tart, pungent ingredient, and much too acid for some stomachs
there is no jovial companionship equal to that where the jokes are rather small, and the laughter abundant

questions.prompt: The Squire and the parson were college friends. What does the narrator mean by calling them “pictures of what men may be made by their different lots in life”?
facilitatorNotes: The Squire went home to his estate and grew “hearty and florid”; the parson “dried and withered away” among books. The same youth led to opposite old ages, shaped by wealth and occupation. Yet the parson’s “alphabet of faces” at the milkmaid story shows a spark left.
Readers can ask whether the narrator thinks circumstance or temperament made the difference; his phrasing (“made by their different lots”) points to circumstance.
evidence: the two college chums presented pictures of what men may be made by their different lots in life
whilst the poor parson, on the contrary, had dried and withered away, among dusty tomes, in the silence and shadows of his study

questions.prompt: How does the narrator signal that the after-dinner drinking has gone far enough, without condemning anyone?
facilitatorNotes: He uses a tide image: “wine and wassail” gain “on the dry land of sober judgment,” the jokes get duller as the laughter gets louder, and the parson dozes with his wig askew. The Squire’s summons to the drawing-room shows his “proper love of decorum.”
The criticism is in the comedy rather than in any stated judgment. Students may compare this light touch with a narrator who would state the moral outright.
evidence: I found the tide of wine and wassail fast gaining on the dry land of sober judgment.
whose joviality seemed always tempered with a proper love of decorum

questions.prompt: At blind-man’s buff the narrator suspects Master Simon of being “not a whit more blinded than was convenient.” What is he suggesting, and how might a reader today see the scene differently?
facilitatorNotes: He suggests that Master Simon, an old bachelor, peeks so that he can chase the prettiest girl and avoid “the smaller game.” The narrator treats it as a joke, calling her “a complete picture of a romp” and Master Simon a “rogue.”

Many readers now will notice that she is thirteen and that the narrator’s amused tone makes light of an adult’s attention to a child. Discuss how a narrator’s tone can invite approval that readers are free to withhold, without assuming the worst of a scene the text presents as innocent fun.
evidence: One fine blue-eyed girl of about thirteen
I suspected the rogue of being not a whit more blinded than was convenient

readings.title: The Christmas Dinner: ghost stories, a masque and the writer’s apology
readings.challenge: Follow how the evening moves from ghost stories to costume to the narrator stepping out of the story to speak to his readers directly.
readings.focus: The past revived as a game, and a writer’s defence of writing to please.
readings.context: Recap: after the Christmas dinner the gentlemen drank and told college stories, and the young people played noisy games led by Master Simon as Lord of Misrule. A masque or mummery was a costumed entertainment with dancing. The Covenanters were seventeenth-century Scottish Presbyterians; Kendal green is a woodsman’s cloth; Robin Hood and Maid Marian were favourite figures of old May games. The young officer and Julia are a courting couple introduced on Christmas Eve. A preceptor is a teacher. The footnotes are Irving’s; the notes they mention are printed at the end of the book.

excerpt.locator: Old Christmas (1886), “The Christmas Dinner,” from the parson’s legends to the end of the sketch, with its footnotes; opens “When I returned to the drawing-room, I found the company seated round the fire, listening…”; closes “[Footnote P: See Note K.]”.

questions.prompt: The Squire is “not superstitious himself” but loves to hear the crusader’s ghost stories. What does he envy in superstitious people, and how does that fit his love of old customs?
facilitatorNotes: He “lamented that he could not believe” the legends, thinking a superstitious person “must live in a kind of fairyland.” He wants the feeling of the old world without its beliefs, just as his feast keeps the forms of old customs as a kind of play.
Students may find this wistful or self-indulgent. The tales themselves, such as the crusader squeezing between gate bars “as thin as a sheet of paper,” are told with a smile.
evidence: who, though not superstitious himself, was very fond of seeing others so
a superstitious person, he thought, must live in a kind of fairyland

questions.prompt: During the dance of the masquers it seems “as though the old family portraits had skipped down from their frames.” How does this image sum up the whole Christmas visit?
facilitatorNotes: Costumes from many centuries dance together (“the dark ages were cutting pirouettes and rigadoons”), so the past comes alive as a joyful muddle rather than an accurate reconstruction. The narrator also feels that these customs are “posting fast into oblivion.”
The image joins delight and loss. Some readers see Bracebridge Hall as a living tradition; others see a museum the family plays in.
evidence: as though the old family portraits had skipped down from their frames to join in the sport
Different centuries were figuring at cross hands and right and left
these fleeting customs were posting fast into oblivion

questions.prompt: In the last two paragraphs Irving imagines graver readers asking “To what purpose is all this?” How does he answer, and does he really give up teaching?
facilitatorNotes: He says it is “pleasanter to please than to instruct” and claims only to want to amuse. But he ends by hoping to “prompt a benevolent view of human nature,” which is itself a lesson about kindness.

Students can argue that the modesty is genuine, that it is a graceful way to teach without preaching, or that the sketch’s nostalgia is its real argument. The repeated “surely, surely” suggests he cares about the answer.
evidence: To what purpose is all this?--how is the world to be made wiser by this talk?
It is so much pleasanter to please than to instruct--to play the companion rather than the preceptor.
make my reader more in good humour with his fellow-beings and himself
